senses: A leather thong.
A strap used to secure armor.
ety: From late Middle English lainer, lainere, lanyer, from Old French laniere, lasniere (“thong, lash”) (see modern French lanière (“lanyard, strap”)).

senses: One designed to fit onto a surface such as the top of a table.
A stovetop: the top of a range (an appliance that has multiple burners and also an oven).
Located along a bay
examples: Yesterday's hot weather saw bayside beaches and coastal resorts packed, with surf lifesavers reporting 45 rescues across the state.

senses: Having numerous moles (naevi)
examples: You are a little moley on your stomach.

senses: A person who enjoys exposure to sunlight; an avid sunbather.
A strange form, an alien creature.
Synonym of trousered.
examples: From six large buildings, along six different pathways, walk, hobble, or shuffle nearly 250 white-coated and blue-panted figures to the great Central Hall.
An inside contact reports that fashion artists are being told to draw their panted women to "look like lesbians."

senses: That can be renormalized.
More generally, any arbitrarily large earthworm, especially those favored in angling.
A person or creature who prowls in the night-time.
Ecumenical doctrines and practices, especially as manifested in the ecumenical movement.
Property, owndom; possessions.
ety: From earlier mensk, from Middle English menske (“courtesy, honour”), from Old English mennisċu (“the human condition, humanity”) and/or Old Norse menska (“humanity”). More at mennish, mensch.

senses: An official of a Muslim court, of varied importance, initially controlling access to the caliph, but later very powerful; a chamberlain.
ety: The court title derives from Arabic الحَاجِب (al-ḥājib, “chamberlain”). Use of the word to designate a headscarf derives from Arabic حَاجِب (ḥājib, “concealing, covering, eyebrow”), from حَجَبَ (ḥajaba, “to veil, to cover, to screen”) (whence also hijab).
examples: The hajib was always a man of consequence; being close to the caliph he was always in a position to give messages and ask favours and, most of all, he controlled access to his master.
By our period — the mid-ninth century — the office of hajib doubled with that of the head of the palace guard, which signifies, inter alia, that he was one of the Turkish amirs.

senses: Having the appearance of or resembling a priest.
ety: From Middle English prestly; equivalent to priest + -ly.

senses: A member of a cult.
The ability of a pathogen to establish an infection
examples: The reputation for low infectivity of rubella was probably based on failure to recognise rashless cases.

senses: A type of grilled sandwich made of a small loaf of bread, cut horizontally, filled with meat such as salami or ham, cheese or other food.
examples: There’s a communal slate table where patrons can sit and drink shade-grown coffee or eat a panino stuffed with Julia Hermosa’s locally grown arugula and Sprout Creek Farm cheese.

senses: Pressure-driven filtration through a membrane that removes particles of about two nanometres or larger
A French viscount.
ety: From French vicomte. Doublet of vicecomes and viscount.

senses: To some extent.
In part; part of the way; some of the way.
examples: The timetable for May-December 2022 reveals a service partway back to its pre-COVID level.

Containing, or covered with, cities.
examples: Hast any mortal name, / Fit appellation for this dazzling frame? / Or friends or kinsfolk on the citied earth, / To share our marriage feast and nuptial mirth?

senses: Any of several fields of psychology that model brain processes in terms of interconnected networks.
to recite the Jewish liturgy; to pray

examples: We were boldly duochrome in our bear-up black sweatpants and white sleeveless T-shirts with crosses and religious medals dangling from our necks, sort of a City Ballet meets St. Mark's Place kind of look.
Duochrome monotony of gray weather recalling Cage's Four Minutes Thirty-Three Seconds of silence, making Julian hungry to see something with a feeling attached.
A drab series of duochrome fashions reflected the comparatively flat progression of the country through the first half of this century.

senses: A person who has myasthenia.
ety: From myasthenia + -ic. By surface analysis, my- (“muscle”) + a- (“not”) + sthen- (“strength”) + -ic (“adjective suffix”).

senses: That which positions.
Any mechanical device used to position something.
The part of a control valve used to control the opening or closing of the actuator based on electric, or pneumatic signals.
examples: Men and women end up recognising each other not only in their commodities (a car, a mobile phone), but also in their capacity to influence as positioners of these needs and satisfactions (Marcuse 1987).

senses: A supporter of adaptationism.
examples: Until one is clear about just what one means by adaptationism, what evidence one needs to accuse someone of being an "adaptationist" will remain vague; this rather diminishes the force of the accusation.

senses: sweet potato (plant)
sweet potato (foodstuff)
ety: Borrowed from Spanish batata, from Taíno batata. Doublet of potato.

senses: A region ruled by a duke or duchess.
The rank or title of a duke.
ety: From late Middle English dukdom, dukedom; equivalent to duke + -dom.

senses: A member of a sect of ancient physicians who based their theories solely on experience.
Someone who is guided by empiricism; an empiricist.
Any unqualified or dishonest practitioner; a charlatan; a quack.
ety: Borrowed from Latin empiricus, from Ancient Greek ἐμπειρῐκός (empeirĭkós, “experienced”), from ἐμπειρία (empeiría, “experience, mere experience or practice without knowledge, especially in medicine, empiricism”), from ἔμπειρος (émpeiros, “experienced or practised in”), from ἐν (en, “in”) + πεῖρα (peîra, “a trial, experiment, attempt”). Not related to empire.

senses: Within a soil profile, a set of related soil horizons that share the same cycle of pedogenic processes; the upper layers of a soil profile that are affected by climate.
ety: From Latin solum (“base, bottom; soil”). Doublet of soil.

senses: Very successful or profitable.
ety: The adjective and adverb are a shortening of the phrase like gangbusters.
examples: What went wrong for Ophelia Lovibond? It was all looking gangbusters after a string of entry-level Hollywood roles.

senses: divided (within one instrumental part, simultaneous notes between two or more players)
Having an associated prebend.
ety: From Latin praebenda (“the support or allowance afforded by the state to a private person”).

senses: A tree (Calophyllum inophyllum), widely distributed in the Pacific islands, that yields a resin and a bitter oil (tamanol).
European seabass (Dicentrarchus labrax)
Any equation of this kind.
A telegraph that automatically prints transmitted messages in letters rather than Morse code or other symbols, typically resembling a typewriter in appearance.
A telegram produced by this device.
An early input/output device for mainframe computers, resembling a typewriter.
ety: From tele- (“far, distant, telegraph”) + type (“text, typewriter”), q.v. In the United States, chiefly understood as a genericization of the Morkrum or Teletype Corporation's branded teletype machines. Doublet of telotype.

senses: A fore-and-aft rigged sailing vessel with two masts, main and mizzen, the mizzen being stepped forward of the rudder post.
ety: From Middle English catche, from cacchen (“to catch”). For the modern form with /ɛ/, compare the pronunciation /kɛtʃ/ of catch.

senses: A Maori storehouse for food, typically raised above the ground.
examples: The brown grass that Barry cut for us / With the new sickle, is lying in heaps / Between the house and the door of the pataka / Where we stuck our mattresses.
